slides.title: Miscellaneous Math for Graphics
slides.notes: Open by framing the chapter as a reliability layer for graphics, not as a disconnected survey. The learner should hear that every later rendering algorithm depends on small mathematical contracts: valid domains, stable numerical roots, auditable frames, well oriented normals, interpolation weights, and probability densities that keep sampled estimates honest.

slides.title: Each Topic Becomes a Code Contract
slides.notes: Present the roadmap as a sequence of responsibilities. Domains decide whether a calculation is meaningful, stable roots decide whether an intersection is found, frames decide whether orientation and lengths are trustworthy, and probability decides whether a renderer's average converges to the intended quantity rather than to a biased accident.

slides.title: Domains Control Whether Inverses Exist
slides.notes: Emphasize that domain information is not cosmetic notation. A ray routine, texture lookup, or logarithm call has the same issue as the square function: the output can only be interpreted correctly when the allowed inputs and endpoint conventions are explicit. The square example is useful because everyone can see the inverse problem immediately.

slides.title: Intervals Are Small Data Structures
slides.notes: Use this slide to slow down on endpoints. Many graphics algorithms carry an interval for a ray parameter, a clipping window, or a valid texture coordinate range. Whether an endpoint is included can decide if a hit is accepted twice, rejected entirely, or allowed to pass into an inverse such as a logarithm.

slides.title: Algebraically Correct Is Not Always Numerically Stable
slides.notes: Connect the stable quadratic formula directly to graphics practice. A missed small root can mean a ray starts just outside an object but fails to find the first hit, or a visibility query jumps to a farther surface. The residual plot in the notebook is not decoration; it is a practical test for root quality.

slides.title: Trigonometry Supplies Coordinate Conversions
slides.notes: The important teaching move is to connect familiar right-triangle trigonometry to the measurements used in rendering. Cosines measure directional agreement, sines carry area factors, and solid angle explains why light integrals are weighted by directions on a sphere rather than by flat image coordinates alone.

slides.title: Dot And Cross Products Are Geometry Tests
slides.notes: Stress that vector operations are not merely formulas to memorize. The dot product asks how much one direction agrees with another, while the cross product measures an oriented area and supplies a perpendicular direction. Those meanings are what let a renderer test normals, projections, handedness, and frame quality.

slides.title: Build Frames, Then Audit Them
slides.notes: This slide should make the frame checks feel concrete. An orthonormal frame is not guaranteed because three vectors look roughly perpendicular on screen. The Gram matrix tests lengths and dot products, while the determinant detects a left-handed frame that would flip normals, texture orientation, or camera roll.

slides.title: Read An Integral As Amount From Density
slides.notes: Treat integration as a unit-checking activity. Learners should ask what quantity is being accumulated, what domain it is accumulated over, and which measure belongs to that domain. This prevents common graphics mistakes such as treating a probability density, a surface density, or a solid-angle density as if it were already a plain amount.

slides.title: Implicit Geometry Answers: Is This Point On The Shape?
slides.notes: Point out that implicit geometry is excellent when an algorithm needs to ask whether a point satisfies a condition. The gradient gives a normal without explicitly walking over the shape, but the equation can be scaled or negated, so orientation must be chosen deliberately before using the normal in lighting.

slides.title: Parametric Geometry Answers: How Do We Generate Points?
slides.notes: Contrast this with the implicit slide. Parametric geometry is valuable when the renderer needs to generate points, walk along a curve, draw a surface patch, or sample a domain. The two tangent derivatives give local directions, and their cross product supplies a normal whose orientation depends on the chosen parameter order.

slides.title: Lerp Turns A Parameter Into A Point
slides.notes: Make interpolation feel like a data movement rule. The same pair of weights that locates a point on a segment can also move an attribute between endpoint values. That is why linear interpolation reappears in rasterization, depth buffering, texture lookup, animation curves, and shading calculations.

slides.title: Barycentric Coordinates Are Triangle Weights
slides.notes: Explain barycentric coordinates as interpolation weights rather than as abstract triangle algebra. If all three weights are nonnegative and sum to one, the point is inside. If one weight is negative, the point lies outside across the opposite edge. This makes barycentrics a compact language for rasterization and attribute interpolation.

slides.title: PMFs And PDFs Are Bookkeeping Systems
slides.notes: Keep the distinction between discrete and continuous probability explicit. A PMF assigns mass to outcomes, while a PDF assigns density that must be integrated over an interval. This prepares students to understand why renderers divide by the sampling density rather than by a raw count alone.

slides.title: The Estimator Must Match The Sampling Density
slides.notes: The estimator is the heart of the probability portion. Students should read each term aloud: choose samples using density p, evaluate the function, divide by p to remove the sampling preference, and average. Importance sampling is not cheating; it is a change of sampling strategy with a required correction.

slides.title: Average An Attribute Over A Triangle
slides.notes: Use the lab as a synthesis rather than as a separate application. The triangle provides a domain, barycentric coordinates provide weights, probability supplies random points, and Monte Carlo turns the sample values into an estimate. The exact affine average gives a clean correctness target for the experiment.

slides.title: A Graphics Math Checklist
slides.notes: Close by returning to the checklist. Chapter 02 is miscellaneous only in title; the topics form a chain of responsibilities that later graphics code relies on. Encourage students to treat each formula as something with a domain, units, invariants, and failure modes that can be tested before a visual artifact is trusted.
